items.title: Copper at $6.89 a Pound: Why the "Boring" Metal Is 2026's Hottest Trade
items.body:
## A Quiet Metal Suddenly Isn't

For most of its industrial history, copper has been the metal nobody gets excited about. It doesn't glitter like gold, it isn't whispered about at dinner parties like bitcoin, and it doesn't headline finance shows the way tech stocks do. Yet in 2026, copper has quietly done something none of those flashier assets have managed: it has become the best-performing major asset of the year, with futures climbing to roughly $6.89 a pound — an all-time high.

To understand why, you have to look past the price chart and into three overlapping stories: artificial intelligence, electric vehicles, and a supply chain that simply cannot keep up.

## The AI Data Center Boom Needs Wire, Not Chips

Every conversation about artificial intelligence tends to focus on processors and chatbots, but the physical infrastructure behind AI is arguably just as important — and far more copper-intensive than most people realize. Data centers built to train and run large AI models require enormous amounts of electrical wiring, cooling systems, backup power infrastructure, and grid connections, almost all of which rely heavily on copper.

Industry estimates suggest a single large-scale AI data center campus can require several times more copper per unit of power capacity than a traditional data center, largely because of the density of power delivery and cooling needed to support high-performance computing hardware. As tech companies race to build out capacity across the United States, the Gulf region, and Asia, that demand has added a new and fast-growing buyer to a market that was already tight.

## Electric Vehicles Keep Adding Pressure

AI isn't the only demand driver. Electric vehicles use roughly two to three times more copper than a comparable gasoline-powered car, largely due to wiring, motors, and battery systems. Add in the copper needed for EV charging networks and renewable energy infrastructure like wind turbines and solar farms, and it becomes clear why analysts have long flagged copper as a critical bottleneck metal for the broader energy transition — well before AI entered the picture.

## Supply Is Struggling to Keep Up

On the supply side, the picture looks strained. Many of the world's largest copper mines are aging, ore quality at existing sites has been gradually declining, and permitting new mines — particularly in politically sensitive or environmentally protected regions — can take a decade or more. Some major producing countries have also faced operational disruptions, labor disputes, and regulatory delays that have limited near-term output growth.

Layered on top of this is tariff and trade-policy uncertainty. Shifting trade rules and the possibility of new import tariffs have reportedly encouraged some buyers to stockpile copper preemptively, pulling inventory out of the open market and adding another layer of tightness to global supply.

## How Copper Stacks Up Against Gold, Silver, and Bitcoin

What has caught many market watchers off guard is copper's relative performance. Gold and silver have both had strong years, benefiting from safe-haven demand amid economic uncertainty, and bitcoin has seen its own volatile rallies. But by several measures, copper's 2026 gains have outpaced all three, a notable shift for a metal typically viewed as a cyclical industrial commodity rather than a store of value.

This has led some analysts to describe copper as sitting at the intersection of two normally separate narratives: it behaves like an industrial input tied to real-world construction and manufacturing activity, but it is currently being pulled higher by the same futuristic themes — AI infrastructure, electrification — that usually move tech stocks.

## What It Could Mean Going Forward

Higher copper prices tend to ripple outward. Construction costs, electronics manufacturing, home appliances, and vehicle production could all see input costs rise if elevated prices persist. Some manufacturers may accelerate research into copper alternatives or substitution in less critical applications, while others may look to recycling and scrap copper as a way to offset tighter mined supply.

For now, the combination of structural demand growth from AI infrastructure and electrification, alongside supply that adjusts slowly by nature, suggests copper's elevated price environment may not be a short-lived spike. That said, commodity markets are notoriously volatile, and prices can shift quickly with changes in trade policy, industrial demand, or mining output.

## A Reminder, Not a Recommendation

This article is intended as a general overview of market and industry trends and does not constitute financial or investment advice. Commodity prices are volatile and influenced by many unpredictable factors, including geopolitical events, trade policy, and shifts in industrial demand. Anyone considering financial decisions related to commodities, mining stocks, or related markets should consult a licensed financial professional and conduct independent research before acting.

items.title: 30 Days, One Order: Inside the Ruling That Reshapes Google's Ad Tech Business
items.body:
A federal court has handed down one of the most consequential rulings in the history of online advertising, and the clock is now running on what happens next.

## What the Court Decided

In a long-running antitrust case brought by the U.S. Department of Justice and a coalition of state attorneys general, a federal judge ruled that Google illegally monopolized parts of the digital advertising technology market. Rather than ordering the company to break up or sell off pieces of its ad tech business — the most aggressive remedy the government had asked for — the court instead chose a narrower, behavior-focused approach.

Under the order, Google must open its ad exchange, known as AdX, to competing bidding platforms on more equal terms. The company is also required to share certain auction data with publishers, giving website and app owners more visibility into how their ad inventory is priced and sold. The goal is to let rival ad exchanges and buying tools compete on a more level playing field, rather than forcing Google to divest the exchange or its publisher ad server outright.

The judge gave both the Justice Department and Google 30 days to draft the specific language of a final judgment implementing these changes. That means the broad strokes of the ruling are set, but the fine print — timelines, technical specifications, and enforcement mechanisms — is still being negotiated.

## Why the Court Stopped Short of a Breakup

Structural remedies like forced divestitures are rare in U.S. antitrust enforcement because they are difficult to design and can create unintended disruption across an entire industry. Ad tech in particular is a deeply interconnected system: publishers, advertisers, ad exchanges, and measurement tools all depend on shared infrastructure to complete billions of transactions every day.

By opting for interoperability and data-sharing requirements instead of a breakup, the court signaled a preference for remedies that address the specific competitive harms identified during the trial — namely, that Google's control over multiple layers of the ad stack made it difficult for rivals to compete fairly — without unwinding the underlying technology that publishers and advertisers currently rely on.

## What It Means for Publishers, Advertisers, and App Developers

For publishers and app developers who monetize through ad exchanges, the ruling could eventually mean more competition among bidding platforms, potentially better fill rates, and clearer insight into how their inventory is auctioned. Advertisers may see more options for where and how their bids are placed.

That said, meaningful changes are unlikely to arrive overnight. Once the final judgment is drafted, implementation typically involves compliance monitoring, technical integration work, and a phase-in period. Analysts following the case expect the practical effects to unfold gradually over the coming months rather than all at once.

## The Road Ahead

Both sides are expected to use the 30-day window to negotiate the precise wording of the judgment, and disagreements over details are common even after a ruling on remedies has been issued. Google has indicated it may appeal aspects of the underlying liability finding, a process that could take years to resolve even as the remedies move forward in the meantime.

The case is being watched closely well beyond the advertising industry. It represents one of the first major tests of how U.S. courts will address monopoly power in digital markets in the current era of antitrust enforcement, and the outcome could influence how regulators approach other technology platforms going forward.

For now, the immediate story is procedural: a court-ordered deadline, a negotiation between two well-resourced legal teams, and an industry waiting to see exactly what the new rules of the road will look like once the ink dries on the final judgment.

items.title: $103,265 and Rising: Inside the Push to Make Trump's H-1B Visa Fee Permanent
items.body:
## A Temporary Order Reaches a Turning Point

Late last year, the Trump administration issued a proclamation imposing a steep new fee — widely reported at around $100,000, and by some tallies closer to $103,265 once existing filing and processing charges are factored in — on new H-1B visa petitions filed by U.S. employers. The order was framed as a temporary measure meant to curb what officials described as overuse of the program by firms that rely heavily on outsourced technical labor.

Now, as that temporary authority approaches its expiration date, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is reportedly moving to convert the fee into a permanent feature of the H-1B system through formal federal rulemaking. That shift — from an emergency executive action to a lasting regulation — has reopened a debate that touches nearly every corner of the American economy that depends on specialized foreign talent.

## What the H-1B Program Does

The H-1B is the primary visa category U.S. employers use to hire foreign professionals in "specialty occupations" — roles typically requiring a bachelor's degree or higher in fields such as computer science, engineering, medicine, and advanced research. Congress caps the program at 65,000 new visas annually, plus an additional 20,000 for applicants with U.S. master's degrees, and demand routinely exceeds supply, forcing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to run a lottery each year.

Historically, filing fees for an H-1B petition ran in the hundreds to low thousands of dollars, depending on employer size and additional fraud-prevention or training charges. A jump into six-figure territory represents an enormous departure from that baseline — one large enough, critics say, to functionally price many employers out of the program altogether.

## The Administration's Rationale

Officials backing the fee have argued it addresses long-standing concerns that some staffing and outsourcing firms use the H-1B program to bring in workers at wages below what comparable American employees would command, undercutting domestic hiring in technical fields. Under this reasoning, a substantially higher cost per petition would discourage bulk or speculative filings and push employers toward hiring qualified U.S. workers first, reserving H-1B sponsorship for cases where specialized skills genuinely cannot be sourced domestically.

Making the fee permanent via a DHS rule, rather than relying on a temporary proclamation, would also give the policy a firmer legal footing and reduce the uncertainty of having it lapse or face expedited court challenges as an emergency order.

## Pushback From Employers and Universities

Opposition has come from a broad coalition: major technology companies, biotech and pharmaceutical firms, research universities, and hospital systems that sponsor H-1B visas for physicians and specialists. Their central argument is economic and competitive — that a $100,000-plus upfront cost per hire disproportionately burdens startups, academic institutions, and smaller research labs that cannot absorb the expense the way the largest tech companies can, even as global competition for AI, semiconductor, and biomedical talent intensifies.

Universities and nonprofit research institutions have also raised concerns about recruiting international scientists and postdoctoral researchers, a population that has historically been central to U.S. leadership in advanced research fields. Immigration attorneys note that many H-1B sponsors are not the outsourcing firms the policy targets, but ordinary employers filling specialized, hard-to-fill roles.

## The Legal and Political Road Ahead

Converting a presidential proclamation into a standing DHS regulation is not a simple administrative formality. Rulemaking under U.S. law typically requires a public notice-and-comment process, during which businesses, universities, unions, and advocacy groups can formally submit objections or support. That process creates an opening for legal challenges arguing the fee exceeds the agency's statutory authority, conflicts with congressional intent on visa fee-setting, or was adopted without adequate economic justification.

Business groups and immigration law organizations have signaled they are prepared to challenge a finalized rule in court, similar to past disputes over changes to skilled-worker visa policy. Meanwhile, supporters of stronger restrictions on the program are pushing DHS to finalize the rule quickly, arguing that any lapse would return the system to what they view as an exploitable status quo.

## What It Means Going Forward

For now, employers face significant uncertainty: whether to continue sponsoring new H-1B hires at a dramatically higher cost, delay hiring decisions until the rule's fate is clearer, or explore alternative visa categories and offshore hiring arrangements instead. The outcome of this rulemaking fight is likely to shape not only how U.S. companies compete for global talent, but also how future administrations use — or are limited in using — executive authority over the immigration system's fee structure.

The debate is expected to play out over the coming months as DHS moves through the formal rulemaking process, with both sides preparing for what could become one of the more closely watched immigration policy fights of the year.
